questions.title: Error Handling practice 1
questions.prompt: Which block runs whether try succeeds or fails?
choices: finally
catch only
throw
return
questions.explanation: A finally block runs after the try and any matching catch, making it suitable for cleanup that both paths require.

questions.title: Error Handling practice 2
questions.prompt: What is wrong with an empty catch block?
choices: It hides the failure and its evidence
Catch requires a return value
It retries forever
It converts the error to text
questions.explanation: The program silently continues, so neither the user nor the developer can see that save failed or why it failed.

questions.title: Trace Error Handling
questions.prompt: What output does this code produce? Enter each line in order.
questions.explanation: JSON.parse throws before the Loaded message, so catch provides a controlled response. The resulting output is 'Could not read that JSON'.

questions.title: Error Handling practice 5
questions.prompt: What is the problem with `try { riskyWork(); } catch (error) {}`?
choices: The empty catch swallows the failure, so the program looks like it succeeded
An empty catch block is a syntax error
catch cannot take a parameter named error
try requires a finally block to run
questions.explanation: An empty catch discards the error, so a failed `riskyWork()` leaves no trace and the code continues as if all was well. The better version at least logs it and re-throws so a caller who can handle it still gets the chance. An empty catch is legal syntax, `error` is a fine parameter name, and `finally` is optional.

questions.title: Small try blocks
questions.prompt: What is a safer way to shape a JavaScript `try` block?
choices: Keep it close to the operation whose failure the code understands.
Catch every error and hide the message.
Wrap code that cannot fail in a broad try block.
Handle an error where no recovery is possible.
questions.explanation: A smaller `try` block makes it clear which operation is expected to fail. Wrapping a whole app can turn programmer mistakes into vague expected-failure messages, which makes the real bug harder to find.

questions.title: Expected failures
questions.prompt: Which operation deserves protection with error handling?
choices: Replace a useful error with a vague one.
Protect only operations you expect can fail.
Continue as if required data loaded successfully.
Show the same message for every failure.
questions.explanation: Protect operations that can reasonably fail, such as parsing input, loading data, or calling a service. A `try/catch` should communicate the expected failure path, not cover random code just in case.

questions.title: Reading error details
questions.prompt: What should a useful JavaScript error handler inspect?
choices: Ignore the error name and message.
Catch programming mistakes and pretend they are user mistakes.
Read the Error name and message.
Put unrelated operations in one protected block.
questions.explanation: The error name and message usually say what kind of failure happened and where to begin debugging. Ignoring those details leads to generic responses that do not help users or developers.

questions.title: Recovery path
questions.prompt: After catching a failed save or load, what should the UI offer?
choices: Retry without changing the failed condition.
Swallow an error before logging useful context.
Mix validation errors with network errors.
Give users a specific recovery path.
questions.explanation: A handler should guide the next step: retry, choose another input, show a clear message, or use a safe fallback. Catching the error without a recovery path only hides the failure.

questions.title: Rethrowing errors
questions.prompt: What should a layer do when it catches an error it cannot actually handle?
choices: Rethrow errors the current layer cannot handle.
Throw strings instead of error objects.
Forget to rethrow when the current layer cannot handle the problem.
Use a fallback value that breaks later code.
questions.explanation: Rethrow the error, possibly with added context, so a higher layer can respond. Returning fake success data or swallowing the error makes later code trust work that did not happen.

questions.title: Expected versus real bugs
questions.prompt: What balance should JavaScript error handling aim for?
choices: Report failure after already using invalid data.
Handle expected failures while keeping real programming mistakes visible.
Hide stack traces during development.
Let promise rejections go unhandled.
questions.explanation: Good handlers deal with expected failures while keeping programming mistakes visible during development. That way user-facing problems get a path forward, and real bugs still get fixed instead of hidden.
